new_statements.translation: 2.7.1 Stress. In Dura, stress does not bring about a difference in meaning. In Dura almost all words are monosyllabic. Monosyllabic words such as nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and verbs are pronounced with stress. (31) (a) gu 'thicket', (b) ngo 'bat', (c) chhi 'grass', (d) The~ 'plum', (e) thu 'chilli'. In disyllabic words the stress falls on the first syllable. (32) (a) yong 'potato', (b) kotaa~ 'sugarcane', (c) Tumba 'cucumber', (d) chhaapi 'bayberry', (e) mikha 'light/brightness'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; monosyllables (the bulk of the lexicon) are stressed, and in disyllabic words stress falls on the first syllable, i.e. word-initial stress. Nothing is said about words of three or more syllables. The following section (2.7.2) states that intonation, unlike stress, is meaning-distinguishing (falling = statement, rising = polar question); there is no tone section.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the rule is stated only for mono- and disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated lexical items given as examples). Data elicited 2020-21 (FY 2077/078) in Sundarbazar municipality, Lamjung, in a revival context: the grammar itself says actual speakers number no more than one (researcher Muktinath Ghimire, who learned Dura from the last native speakers), with Dura community resource persons Lok Bahadur Dura, Santamaya Dura and Kamala Dura; phoneme inventory based on M.P. Pokharel's earlier determination.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source is the Nepal Language Commission's 2022 Nepali-medium grammar of Dura (dura1244, Lamjung), compiled in a language-revival setting: by its own account (ch. 1, PDF pp. 26, 29) Dura is moribund with 'actual speakers not more than one', that one being the grammar's researcher Muktinath Ghimire (a non-native custodian who learned Dura from the last native speakers, d. by 2008), assisted by Dura community resource persons in Sundarbazar municipality. It treats Tandrange as a reported dialect (per Ethnologue) but does not describe it. Nagila's 2007-2009 Dura data come from different elderly informants in Duradanda and are reviewed separately; Schorer 2016 (not seen) is the standard reference and should be checked before the entry is finalised.

sources.note: Ch. 2 phonology, sec. 2.7.1 'balaghat (Stress)', printed p. 33 (PDF p. 50): stress does not distinguish meaning; almost all words are monosyllabic and are pronounced stressed; in disyllabic words stress falls on the first syllable (exx. 32a-e yoN 'potato', kotaa~ 'sugarcane', Tumba 'cucumber', chhaapi 'bayberry', mikha 'light'). Sec. 2.7.2: intonation is distinctive (statement vs. polar question). No tone section; suprasegmentals = stress + intonation only.
